schools.summary: Gregory, at the very end of his great commentary, likens himself to a voyager sighting the shore, and hears Job's reply aimed at Leviathan — 'I know Thou canst do all things' against his strength, 'no thought is hid from Thee' against his hidden craft.
Gill answers the objection that Job had vowed silence: he meant only not to complain and self-justify as before, and now, more convinced of his ignorance and sins, could not forbear speaking.

Henry marks the transition — the words of self-justification ended (31:40), those of self-condemnation begun (40:4); Job answers not by contradiction but submission, true repentance beginning in the acknowledgement of truth (2 Tim. 2:25).

Clarke surveys the whole chapter from its opening: Job humbled and accepted, the friends censured, sacrifice and intercession commanded, the captivity turned, the affluence doubled, the family restored, and Job's death at 140.

outliers.note: Reads the close of his own labour through the image of a sea-voyage nearing shore, and interprets Job's reply as a double answer to Leviathan's strength and hidden machinations disclosed by the Protector of the tempted.

schools.summary: Gill keeps the first clause plain — God 'canst do every thing,' shown by creation and its continual sustentation.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'no plan is impracticable to Thee' and fix on 'now': the old knowledge risen to new divinely-worked clearness, so that even the affliction is no injustice but a wise, well-digested counsel of God.
Clarke: 'thy power is unlimited, thy wisdom infinite'; Wesley opens 'no thought withholden' both ways — none of ours hid from his knowledge, none of his hindered from execution.

Henry draws the application: Job once said this passionately, complaining (23:13) 'what his soul desireth, even that he doeth,' but now with pleasure, that God's counsels shall stand and can raise him from his low estate.

themes: I know thou canst do every thing

schools.summary: Clarke: Job echoes God's rebuke (38:2) back on himself — 'Alas, I am the man; I have uttered what I understood not'; Wesley: 'what am I that I should be guilty of such madness,' having spoken of things far above his reach.
Gill supplies 'thou didst say' before the quotation — Job owns himself the foolish man with sorrow and shame; notes Schultens takes the words as spoken by Job of God.
Ellicott argues the verses are best read as a dialogue, Job and the LORD alternately replying, rather than as Job's reflective self-quotation of God's challenge.
Henry: that first word, 'who darkens counsel,' reached Job's conscience; he owns himself ignorant of the divine counsels, which are a great deep, and answered a matter before he heard it.

debates.question: Whose words are 'Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge?' — Job reflectively quoting God's challenge, or a genuine alternating dialogue?

sides.position: Job's penitent self-quotation of God's rebuke at 38:2, applied to himself
part of a dialogue in which Job and the LORD alternately reply, the challenge God's

schools.summary: Gill: Job speaks now in an altered key — not complaining and self-justifying, but in humble entreaty and confession, owning the wisdom, goodness, and justice he had once arraigned.
Wesley reads pure submission: 'Hear and accept my humble confession; I will no more dispute, but beg information'; the challenge God gave Job, Job returns as surrender.

Ellicott assigns 'Hear, I beseech thee' to God, as at 38:3 and 40:7, so the confession of vv.5-6 comes in grandly as Job's answer; the confession of Job is that of every converted man (cf. Paul, Gal. 1:16).
Henry: Job is brought at last to the prayer Elihu taught him, 'that which I see not, teach thou me' — the cross-examiner become a petitioner.

debates.question: Is 'Hear, I beseech thee, and I will speak' spoken by Job in submission, or by God as at 38:3?

sides.position: Job the suppliant, asking only to learn and be taught
God's own summons, answered by Job's confession in the verses following

schools.summary: Gill traces the 'hearing' to ancestors, parents and tutors, and ordinary and extraordinary revelation; 'hearing with the hearing of the ear' denotes close attention.

Clarke: 'in seeing thee, I see myself,' the light that shows God's glory showing Job's vileness; Wesley: knowledge once grounded on men's instruction now immediately inspired, sight exceeding common fame.
Keil and Delitzsch: Job's penitence now perfected — a world of divine wisdom opens before him, his affliction among its mysteries, a wise decree he adoringly bows to yet cannot fathom.

Henry: a mercy to know God by word and ministers, but the Spirit's enlightening exceeds report as sight exceeds fame; God reveals himself most fully by the rebukes of his word and providence — 'the rod and reproof give wisdom.'

themes: hearing of the ear versus sight

schools.summary: Gill (with Aben Ezra) reads the object as 'all my words,' the indecent expressions concerning God, loathed now, and himself for them — sin abominable in its nature, loathsome most when seen against God's holiness and grace.
Clarke widens it to the whole man — strength weakness, wisdom folly, righteousness impurity — distressed for the imaginations of his heart, the words of his tongue, and the acts of his life.
Henry keeps it narrow: Job humbled for his folly and unadvised speaking, for pride, passion, peevishness, and murmuring; self-loathing evermore the companion of true repentance (Ezek. 6:9).
Ellicott had already made Job's confession that of every converted man, a self-abhorrence laid bare before God.

debates.question: Of what does Job repent — his rash speeches in the debate, or himself as a sinner simply?

sides.position: chiefly his folly, impatience, and unadvised speaking in the controversy
himself as a sinner broadly — the confession of every converted man
both the particular indecent words and the sinfulness they betray

schools.summary: Henry seizes the reversal — the verdict for Job, not against him; 'judge nothing before the time.' God calls him 'my servant' four times; Job spoke right by judging God's love and hatred by what is in men, not before them (Eccl. 9:1).

Clarke (with Peters) roots the difference in the doctrine of a future state — Job saw reward and punishment beyond this life, the friends' scheme sapping the proof of it; Wesley: the difference is comparative, not absolute; Eliphaz the eldest and ringleader, Elihu spared.

Ellicott shifts the ground to spirit: the verdict rests on the tone and temper of the friends' advocacy, not their actual words, many of them wise and beautiful; their fault was to think God's cause needed lies (13:7).
Gill marks Eliphaz addressed as eldest and ringleader who led the rest into the same fault.

debates.question: What made the friends 'not speak right' and Job right?

sides.position: the doctrine of a future state — Job referred reward and punishment beyond this life
the tone and spirit of the friends' advocacy, not the substance of their words
a comparative, not absolute, truth about providence's dispensations toward good and bad

themes: ye have not spoken the thing that is right

schools.summary: Gill: sacrifices used before the Levitical law, the number Balaam offered in Moab; typical of Christ, the strong bullocks and the sevenfold number pointing at the perfection of the one atoning sacrifice.

Ellicott: the offering matches Balaam's for Balak (Num. 23:2), a mark that Job's age was Moses' or before; Job's intercession makes him a type of Christ, the book anticipating the Gospel to the Gentiles. Keil and Delitzsch parse 'right' as 'correct' (not 'sincere'), blending objective truth and truthfulness.

Clarke: a full proof of Job's innocence — priest for his accusers as once for his children (1:5), God clearing his character; Wesley: 'my servant, whom you condemned as hypocrite, I own... whom I constitute your priest.'

outliers.note: Reads Job's intercession typologically — his character representing Christ the sufferer and mediator, and the book, lacking any trace of the covenant, an anticipation of the Gospel to the Gentile world under a universal principle of mediation.

schools.summary: Gill: having taken the appointed creatures, they went to Job — the instructors now coming to be prayed for.
Henry: good men, they obeyed speedily and without gainsaying, though it went against flesh and blood; peace with God is had only in his own way; those who sinned together must repent together.
Keil and Delitzsch: Jehovah risen as witness for Job, the spiritual redemption already accomplished; only the outward, visible showing of himself as the righteous One remains.

Wesley: as Job prayed and sacrificed for those who wounded his spirit, so Christ prayed and died for his persecutors; Henry adds God 'accepted Job' for them, we made accepted in the beloved (Eph. 1:6).

themes: they did as the LORD commanded

schools.summary: Gill: not literal or spiritual captivity, but restoration from affliction to a happy state — substance, health, friends, and deliverance out of Satan's hand.

Keil and Delitzsch: the word is 'when,' not 'because' — praying for his friends became the turning-point of glory (the Talmud's proverb); Ellicott: his discipline was not complete till he passed from his own sorrows to intercession — the true moral of all human history.

Henry: mercy returned not while Job disputed but while he prayed for his friends; God better pleased with warm devotions than warm disputations; the doubled estate balances his losses and rewards his confidence (Heb. 10:35; James 5:11).

Clarke notes the Vulgate ('turned Job to repentance') and Chaldee ('the Word of the Lord') and presses that mercy is shown only to the merciful — 'he who can pray for another cannot entertain enmity'; dismisses the spoil-the-spoilers guess. Wesley: the distempers healed, probably in a moment.

outliers.note: Records the Vulgate and Chaldee variant renderings of the clause and explicitly rejects the supposition that Job armed his servants and plundered the spoilers to recover his wealth, finding no intimation of it in the text.

themes: mercy when he prayed for his friends

schools.summary: Gill takes the 'brethren and sisters' in the larger sense of all his kindred and kinsfolk.

Keil and Delitzsch: prosperity gathered those calamity had scattered, human love but shades of selfishness, yet Job does not thrust them back; Ellicott handles the kesitah cautiously — found at Gen. 33:19, reckoned by some at four shekels, by tradition a lamb-stamped coin.

Clarke (with Heath): a striking view of human friendship, each bringing a kesitah by eastern custom; the word means a lamb, so the versions, perhaps a coin stamped with a lamb (Gen. 33:19). Wesley sets the visit when God was reconciled, the feasting congratulation, the bemoaning long-felt sympathy.
Henry calls them swallow-friends gone in winter and back in spring, yet owns God put it in their hearts, their gifts the small seed of a great estate.

debates.question: Was the kesitah an actual lamb or a piece of money?

sides.position: a lamb or sheep given in kind, as the ancient versions render it
a coin, named from the figure of a lamb stamped upon it

themes: a piece of money and a golden earring

schools.summary: Gill: the fulfilment of Bildad's conditional supposition; the last days of a good man sometimes his best — 'the best wine is reserved till last.'

Keil and Delitzsch confirm the exact doubling of the numbers at 1:3; Ellicott turns the doubling on the verdict — the friends promised Job's blessed end (5:24; 8:7) but hampered with a condition implying the falsehood of his life.
Clarke (with Heath) makes the friends' presents the natural means of the sudden increase; Wesley reads the exact doubling as a wonder of providence extending to the tale of a man's cattle.
Henry: 'the blessing of the LORD makes rich'; the last works of a good man often his best, his path shining more and more unto the perfect day.

debates.question: Did the doubled wealth come by God's direct blessing or through the friends' gifts as its means?

sides.position: the natural consequence of the friends' presents of cattle and gold
the direct blessing of God, the exact doubling a token of special favour

outliers.note: Following Heath, rationalizes the sudden doubling as the natural fruit of the kinsfolk's contributions of sheep, cattle, and gold, and reinterprets their visit as prompted by the proof of Job's vindication rather than by his prosperity.

themes: the latter end blessed more than the beginning

schools.summary: Gill: same number and kind as before; reports Nachman's 'the very same,' the Targum's fourteen sons, the doubling-in-quality and the immortality readings — but warns 'these senses are not to be trusted.'

Keil and Delitzsch embrace what Gill distrusts: the equal number is itself a doubling, the dead children not absolutely lost (2 Sam. 12:23); note the archaic pausal 'seven' from the primeval-history style (Gen. 21:29; Ruth 1:19).
Clarke: the same number as before (so Vulgate, LXX, Syriac, Arabic), the Chaldee alone doubling the sons to fourteen.

debates.question: Why are the children only equalled, not doubled like the cattle?

sides.position: the equal number is the truest doubling — the deceased children are not lost but gathered
the doubling touches only the substance and cattle; the children are simply the same number again

outliers.note: Notes the Chaldee (Targum) alone reads fourteen sons, doubling them against the same number given by the Hebrew and the other versions.

schools.summary: Gill reads Jemima as 'the day' (Targum), noting also the Arabic sense of a turtle-dove and an Arabian country and queen of the name.

Wesley: Jemima 'the day' from her beauty or her birth in the day of prosperity, Kezia cassia, Keren-happuch 'plenty restored'; Clarke reads Keren-happuch as the cornucopia, the horn of plenty, and records the versions' variety (Amalthea's horn, antimony, Coverdale).

Keil and Delitzsch: Jemima a dove (dove's eyes), Kezia cassia, Keren-happuch a horn of paint — the youngest the fairest, beauty heightened by art, the three like the Graces; Ellicott: Keren-happuch the kohl paint-horn (2 Kings 9:30; Jer. 4:30), Kezia the cassia of Ps. 45:9, Jemima 'fair as the day.'

sides.position: the flowing horn, cornucopia, the horn of plenty
the horn for eye-paint (kohl), a cosmetic of beauty

themes: horn of plenty or horn of paint

schools.summary: Gill reads the beauty broadly, of the whole world or the country, with a spiritual turn — the children of Christ (Job's antitype) all fair, without spot or wrinkle.

Wesley: women praised for beauty in the Old Testament but never in the New, the beauty of holiness now brought to clearer light; Clarke refers the daughters' inheritance to the daughters of Zelophehad (Num. 27), first allowed a share among their brethren.

Keil and Delitzsch: the inheritance sounds more Arabian than Israelite, the Law granting daughters a share only where there are no sons (Num. 27:8); the writer is telling an extra-Israelite, pre-Mosaic history.
Henry: the daughters must have had extraordinary merit, excelling in wisdom and piety, so Job made them co-heirs rather than turn them off with small portions.

debates.question: Is Job's giving daughters inheritance among sons a pre-Mosaic custom or an echo of Zelophehad's daughters?

sides.position: a pre-Mosaic, extra-Israelite custom, the Law granting daughters a share only where there are no sons (Num. 27:8)
an echo of the daughters of Zelophehad, first allowed inheritance among their brethren (Num. 27)

schools.summary: Gill weighs the doubled-age view (seventy at the trial, two hundred and ten in all, the Jewish notion) against a soberer reckoning of fifty or sixty at the time and about two hundred years in all — a singular blessing beside Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Joshua.

Clarke: we cannot tell how long Job lived before; the LXX adds a total of two hundred and forty (a hundred at the trial), Coverdale reads only forty after; from the Hebrew nothing can be inferred about his date.
Keil and Delitzsch mark the primeval-history cadence kept to the last, the four generations echoing the patriarchs' close (Gen. 50:23).
Henry: though the children were not doubled, in his children's children they were more than doubled; God repairs the losses of a man written childless, as he gave Adam another seed (Gen. 4:25).

debates.question: What was the sum of Job's days and his age at the trial?

sides.position: his age was doubled — seventy at the trial, two hundred and ten in all (the Jewish reckoning)
the Septuagint's two hundred and forty years in all, a hundred at the trial
indeterminate — the Hebrew lets us infer nothing about his date or total age

schools.summary: Gill: Job died as all must, as Methuselah and the best of men die, yet a good man in the Lord, in faith and hope of eternal life, and in outward prosperity with a numerous offspring.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'old and weary of life,' beside the patriarchs (Gen. 25:8; 35:29): a New Testament poet would have ended with Job waving the palm of victory before the throne, but the Old Testament poet could not, Job's hope beyond death a purely individual aspiration of faith. Ellicott closes on the book's argument — the foiling of Satan's malice, since the restoration was hidden from Job till his probation ended; Job named but twice more (Ezek. 14:14; James 5:11).

Clarke: Job had seen life in all its varieties, risen higher and sunk lower than any, and died satisfied with life; in him the whole history of Providence was exemplified, the end of the Lord very pitiful (James 5:11).

outliers.note: Reflects that a New Testament poet would have closed the book with Job triumphant before the throne among those who washed their robes white, whereas the Old Testament poet, able to open in heaven, could not so end, Job's hope of acknowledgement after death remaining an individual aspiration of faith.
